stem.text: A function f has derivative \( f'(x) = 4\left(x + 2\right)\left(x - 1\right) \) for all real x. On what open intervals is f decreasing? Give a reason for the answer.

answer_key.label: f is decreasing on the interval \( (-2, 1) \), because \( f'(x) < 0 \) on that interval.

worked_solution.text: The sign of f' can change only where \( f'(x) = 0 \) at \( x = -2 \) and \( x = 1 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: partition points of the sign chart

worked_solution.text: Testing one point in each piece gives \( f'(x) < 0 \) on the interval \( (-2, 1) \) and \( f'(x) > 0 \) on the intervals \( (-\infty, -2) \) and \( (1, \infty) \).
So f is decreasing on the interval \( (-2, 1) \), because \( f'(x) < 0 \) on that interval.
worked_solution.rule_named: sign of the derivative gives the direction of the function

options.label: f is decreasing on the intervals \( (-\infty, -2) \) and \( (1, \infty) \), because \( f'(x) < 0 \) on each of those intervals.
options.derivation: the sign of f' read backwards, so the pieces where f' has the opposite sign are reported

options.label: f is decreasing on the interval \( (-\infty, - \frac{1}{2}) \), because f' is decreasing there.
options.derivation: f taken to be decreasing where f' is decreasing, on the side of x = -1/2 where f'' has that sign

options.label: f is decreasing on the interval \( (-2, 1) \), because \( f'(x) < 0 \) on that interval.
f is decreasing on the interval \( (-2, 1) \), because it is negative there.
